Algorithm explanations and C reference materials

Start with one prefix calculation

Section titled “Start with one prefix calculation”

A prefix is the part of a name read so far. A dynamic-programming table saves answers for those smaller parts, then reuses them. For cat and cut, the cell for ca and cu compares deletion, insertion and replacement. Their costs are 2, 2 and 1. That cell stores 1, and the final matching t adds zero.

Lloyd Allison’s edit-distance explanation connects those three choices to table cells and recycled rows. Read the recurrence, then the two-row storage note. Our shared routine keeps a third row for adjacent swaps. Jeff Erickson’s dynamic-programming chapter, section 3.7, develops the same prefix reasoning with edit alignments. These references explain the method; the examples and comments here are written for this project’s C implementation.

Distinguish the two adjacent-swap distances

Section titled “Distinguish the two adjacent-swap distances”

Optimal String Alignment, often abbreviated OSA, means the restricted adjacent-letter-swap method here. A swapped substring cannot be edited again under its recurrence. Full Damerau-Levenshtein allows further edits. Both count ab -> ba as one edit. Only the full method finds ca -> ac -> abc at cost 2; the restricted method returns 3.

RapidFuzz’s restricted-method reference documents its distance and normalization. Its full-method reference includes the CA to ABC example. These are comparison definitions, not runtime dependencies. The full recurrence is described by Lowrance and Wagner in An Extension of the String-to-String Correction Problem. In our source, the important extra state is the last occurrence of each letter.

Count matched letters and shared starts

Section titled “Count matched letters and shared starts”

NIST’s Jaro-Winkler entry describes the matched-character family and the preference for matching starts. Our Jaro article shows the three fractions for martha and marhta. Our Winkler adapter uses the explicitly documented variant: a 0.1 prefix factor, at most four letters, only when the base score exceeds 0.7. A shared start is evidence of similar spelling, not of equal configuration meaning.

Separate ordered letters from contiguous blocks

Section titled “Separate ordered letters from contiguous blocks”

NIST’s longest-common-subsequence definition explains why gaps are allowed: abc and ac share the sequence ac. The word “longest” means the method keeps as many letters as possible while retaining order. The source function is named lcs_score; LCS expands to longest common subsequence.

NIST’s Ratcliff/Obershelp entry describes selecting a common block and repeating on its two sides. A block must be contiguous. Our implementation fixes tie orientation and uses an explicit stack; its score is 2 * selected letters / total letters. Those implementation choices are stated beside the code.

Compare windows as sets or frequency vectors

Section titled “Compare windows as sets or frequency vectors”

Manning, Raghavan and Schutze’s Introduction to Information Retrieval, section 19.6 explains shingles and Jaccard overlap. Their example uses word windows; this project uses character windows. Our exact gram extraction, boundary policy and Dice coefficient are defined in the source article rather than borrowed from their preprocessing.

Section 6.3.1 on dot products explains cosine as a normalized dot product. Here each coordinate counts one trigram. The worked aaaba versus aaaa table shows why repeated windows matter to cosine but not set overlap.

Recognize project-specific variants

Section titled “Recognize project-specific variants”

Weighted edit costs and the ordered-token hybrid are experiments defined here. The edit-distance recurrence supplies the mechanism; horizontal keyboard neighbors, digit costs and the 65/35 mixture are fixed project choices. They are not universal rules endorsed by the linked references. The hybrid aligns words in order, using character edit costs to price a misspelled word.

Read C storage and library calls

Section titled “Read C storage and library calls”

The public C99 committee draft with technical corrigenda, N1256 is the reference for language and standard-library contracts. Section 6.5.6 covers pointer arithmetic; section 7.4 covers character classification; section 7.21.2 covers memcpy and memmove; section 7.20.1 covers numeric conversion; section 7.20.5 covers searching and sorting; section 7.23 covers time. It is a reference document, so use the named section rather than reading it end to end.

memmove handles overlapping source and destination ranges. memcpy requires non-overlapping ranges and copies exactly the requested bytes. Character-classification functions require an unsigned-char value or EOF. strtol reports the first unconsumed character as well as range errors. Comments explain those contracts at their call sites.

The POSIX clock_gettime reference documents the monotonic clock used on this host. The isolated fallback uses C99 clock() and measures CPU time instead of elapsed wall time.

Write comments that explain a decision or representation

Section titled “Write comments that explain a decision or representation”

The Linux kernel commenting section emphasizes purpose and reasons and discourages redundant commentary. We apply that restraint, while explaining unfamiliar calculations and storage details needed by learners. The repository’s AGENTS.md records the rules for future changes. A useful comment answers a concrete question: “What does this cell store?”, “Why is this index one larger?”, or “Why must this copy include the terminator?”
